blocks.note: a smart is a sharp stinging pain

annotation.surface: A know-it-all American getting what's coming to him.

entries.clue: Loom has one political figure on arse (6)

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a Member of Parliament

annotation.surface: A politician sitting down on a weaving machine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loom' looks like the weaving frame the MP might sit on, but it is the verb: to hang over threateningly.

entries.clue: A 'dish' can when mounting Stephen? (4-3)

annotation.surface: A crude joke about an attractive person and the comedian Stephen Fry in prison.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'dish' invite the slang sense of an attractive person; it is just a meal. Can and stir are both British slang for prison, and prison is where the surface's mounting would happen.
annotation.definitionFit: A stir-fry is a dish of food fried quickly in a wok.

entries.clue: see 11ac. (7)

annotation.definition: At the end of the day

indicatorNotes.corruption: a corrupted text has its letters garbled
indicatorNotes.hiding: the outer letters hide the rearranged word between them
indicatorNotes.extremes: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of market
the letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A glum verdict that, when all's said and done, the market is corrupt behind closed doors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At the end of the day' pretends to be the stock phrase meaning 'ultimately', but it is literal: the day ends at midnight. 'Hiding' does double work as the letters and as the word that puts them inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Midnight is the moment one day ends and the next begins.

entries.clue: Where to pick up someone for sex – hopefully with no trace of stallion? (4,6)

annotation.definition: Where to pick up someone for sex – hopefully with no trace of stallion?

blocks.clueFragment: Where to pick up someone for sex
blocks.note: slang for a bar or club where people size each other up as sexual partners

blocks.clueFragment: hopefully with no trace of stallion
blocks.note: a place selling butchers' produce, which after the 2013 horsemeat scandal should contain no horse

annotation.surface: A pick-up joint whose clientele, one hopes, includes no studs.
annotation.walkthrough: A stallion is also slang for a virile man, so the surface keeps the pick-up scene going; the other reading is a butcher's market after the 2013 horsemeat scandal.
annotation.definitionFit: Meat market is slang for a singles bar where people are sized up like cuts of meat.

entries.clue: Gordonstoun for Charles: "big battle with mama" (4,5)

blocks.note: the Battle of the Alma, 1854, was the first big battle of the Crimean War
mater is Latin for mother, used as old public-school slang for one's mum

annotation.surface: King Charles recalling his boarding school as a war zone with his mother in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: Gordonstoun is the tough Scottish boarding school King Charles attended and famously hated, so the quoted 'big battle' reads as his verdict on it.
annotation.definitionFit: Your alma mater is the school or university you attended, and Gordonstoun was Charles's.

entries.clue: see 23ac. (5)
Hunt, Tory, oddly boring thing (5)

indicatorNotes.oddly: take the odd-numbered letters, the first and third

blocks.note: letters one and three of Tory
an awl is a pointed tool for boring holes

annotation.surface: A jibe at Jeremy Hunt as an odd Conservative who bores everyone.
annotation.walkthrough: Hunt reads as Jeremy Hunt, the Conservative minister, and 'boring' as dull; it is the verb 'to hunt' and a hole-making tool.
annotation.definitionFit: To trawl through something is to hunt through it thoroughly.

entries.clue: (& 5dn.) Driving a hard bargain, apparently supermarkets' business now? (5)

blocks.note: shrewd, tough haggling, named after the sharp practice of old dealers in a certain animal
in 2013 British supermarkets were found selling beef products that contained horsemeat

annotation.surface: A dig at supermarkets both squeezing their suppliers and, it seems, selling horse.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue dates from the 2013 horsemeat scandal, when meat sold as beef in British supermarkets turned out to be horse. The answer runs on into 5 down.
annotation.definitionFit: Horse trading is hard, shrewd bargaining, named after the old reputation of horse dealers.

entries.clue: 'Superfluous' Brown interrupting Miliband during tirade? (9)

indicatorNotes.interrupting: something that interrupts gets in the middle, so DUN goes between the E and D
indicatorNotes.during: what happens during something falls inside it, so the whole lot goes inside RANT

blocks.note: a rant is a tirade
Ed Miliband, Labour leader from 2010 to 2015
dun is a dull greyish brown

annotation.surface: Gordon Brown butting in on Ed Miliband mid-rant, as the old leader no longer needed.
annotation.walkthrough: Brown is Gordon Brown, the former Labour prime minister, which is why calling him superfluous stings; here he is only a colour.
annotation.definitionFit: Something redundant is no longer needed: superfluous.

entries.clue: see 27dn. (7)
Can they be sure they really are? – er, safe bet processed contains substitute, ultimately (10)

annotation.definition: Can they be sure they really are?

indicatorNotes.processed: processed food has been broken down and reshaped
indicatorNotes.contains: the rearranged letters hold the next piece inside
indicatorNotes.ultimately: the last letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
the last letter of substitute

annotation.surface: A hesitant question about whether something processed is a safe bet.
annotation.walkthrough: Beefeaters are the guards at the Tower of London; after the horsemeat scandal no beef eater could be sure the beef was beef. 'Processed' and 'substitute' keep the adulterated-meat theme going.
annotation.definitionFit: The question plays on the name: a beefeater eats beef, but nobody could be sure their beef was genuine.

entries.clue: Issue raised by one-time minister Cook on the box (7)

blocks.note: the issue is a daughter of Nigel Lawson, Chancellor of the Exchequer in the 1980s
that same daughter is a famous British television cook

annotation.surface: A political row over something former minister Robin Cook said on television.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One-time minister Cook' reads as Robin Cook, Labour's Foreign Secretary; the break falls between them, and Cook is a TV chef.
annotation.definitionFit: Nigella Lawson is both Nigel Lawson's child and a cook who presents television shows.

entries.clue: Standard aspect of Queen's ignorance (6)

indicatorNotes.aspect of: an aspect is one part of a thing, so the answer is a part of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of Queen's into the start of ignorance

annotation.surface: A remark on the royal lack of knowledge being normal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Standard' reads as an adjective meaning typical, but it is a noun: a flag.
annotation.definitionFit: An ensign is a flag, and a standard is a flag too.

entries.clue: Kray type, Reg, bent and full of dread (8)

indicatorNotes.bent: something bent is out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.full of: the rearranged letters are filled with what follows

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
angst is anxious dread

annotation.surface: Reg Kray, one of the gangster twins, crooked and frightening.
annotation.walkthrough: Reg and Ronnie Kray were twin gangsters who ruled London's East End in the 1960s, so 'Reg, bent' reads as a description of him; bent is also British slang for corrupt.
annotation.definitionFit: The Kray twins were the best-known British gangsters.

entries.clue: Smear right inside rump? (6)

indicatorNotes.inside: the R goes inside the next word

blocks.note: rump is a cut of steak, hence the question mark
R is the usual abbreviation for right

annotation.surface: A rude image of a mark left on a backside.
annotation.walkthrough: The rump looks like a bottom, which the smear suits; it is a cut of beef, and the question mark admits that rump is only an example of steak.
annotation.definitionFit: A streak is a long smear or stripe of something.

entries.clue: Trio messed with sex, catching cold: no spirit once one has performed? (8)

annotation.definition: no spirit once one has performed?

indicatorNotes.messed: letters messed with are thrown out of order
indicatorNotes.catching: the rearranged letters catch the C and hold it inside

blocks.note: the first set of letters to rearrange
added to the pile

annotation.surface: A threesome that ends in a chill and a total loss of spirit afterwards.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a deflated threesome; 'spirit' is really a ghost or demon, and 'performed' is an exorcism.
annotation.definitionFit: An exorcist drives spirits out, so once he has performed there is no spirit left.

entries.clue: Is present name bestowed on duke in naff taste? (7)

indicatorNotes.bestowed on: N is given to D, so the two go side by side
indicatorNotes.in: the pair go inside what follows
indicatorNotes.naff: naff is British slang for tacky or useless, so the letters are badly arranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
N is the abbreviation for name
D is the abbreviation for duke

annotation.surface: A title handed to a duke in poor taste, an honours-list sneer.
annotation.walkthrough: Naff is British slang for tacky or tasteless, so 'naff taste' reads as one phrase; it splits into an anagram signal and its letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who turns up in person at an event is there, and the verb for that is to attend.

entries.clue: It stimulates transport (7)

blocks.note: a stimulant party drug, often called E

annotation.surface: A slogan for something that gets vehicles moving.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Transport' reads as buses and trains, but here it means rapture, as in 'transports of delight'.
annotation.definitionFit: Ecstasy is both a stimulant drug and a state of rapture.

entries.clue: Next IT development swamps Conservative, quite the dinosaur (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a phrase describing a state, so it stands for the adjective: to be quite the dinosaur is to be extinct.

indicatorNotes.development: a development changes the shape of things, so the letters are reworked
indicatorNotes.swamps: the rearranged letters swamp the C, closing over it

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

annotation.surface: New computing overwhelming an old-fashioned Tory who is hopelessly out of date.
annotation.walkthrough: A dinosaur is a person with outdated ideas, which the surface applies to the Conservative; the definition takes it literally.
annotation.definitionFit: The dinosaurs are the classic example of a species that has died out.

entries.clue: Privates' "handle", small length, covered with trifle (5)

indicatorNotes.covered with: the millimetres are covered on both sides by the other word, so they sit inside it

blocks.note: to toy with something is to trifle with it

annotation.surface: A smutty remark about a very short penis wrapped in a dessert.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Privates' reads as genitals, and the surface runs with it; they are private soldiers, whose nickname, or handle, is Tommy. A trifle is a British layered dessert.
annotation.definitionFit: Tommy, from Tommy Atkins, has been the nickname for the British private soldier since the First World War.

entries.clue: (&9ac /1dn.) Say you're a gay somewhere off eastern England, would the stain thus disappear? (4,3)

blocks.note: to come out is to tell people you are gay
the Wash is the square bay of the North Sea between Lincolnshire and Norfolk

annotation.surface: A muddled question linking a coming-out to a coastline and a laundry stain.
annotation.walkthrough: The Wash is a large bay on England's east coast, so a place off that coast is 'in the Wash'. The answer runs on into 9 across and 1 down.
annotation.definitionFit: A stain that comes out in the wash disappears when laundered, and the idiom says a problem will sort itself out in the end.

entries.clue: Jingle right by Fanny's entrance almost (5)
